title: Imminent rapid decline of the Indonesian Throughflow after reaching a turning point of CO2 concentration

paper_content.abstract: The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) represents the only tropical inter-ocean pathway of global ocean circulation and plays a central role in the Earth’s climate system. Climate models suggest that the ITF would be weakened under global warming, but historical observations indicate a contradictory trend. Here using CMIP6 simulations, we find that the response of the ITF to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration is nonlinear and exhibits an abrupt rapid decline after surpassing a turning point. The ITF’s decline can be explained by the response of its halosteric and thermosteric components to rising CO2 levels associated with changes in winds and precipitation. The current level of CO2 concentration has reached the turning point, indicating that a rapid decline of ITF and a transition of the Indo-Pacific state is likely imminent despite the remaining uncertainties. These findings have implications for understanding climate tipping elements and global ocean circulation under global warming.
paper_content.introduction:
The Indo-Pacific region is the only pathway that connects different ocean basins in the tropics and plays a central role in the Earth’s climate system1–3. The cross-basin oceanic flow from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean, termed the Indonesian Throughflow (ITF), controls the inter-ocean exchange of heat and fresh water between the Pacific Ocean and Indian Ocean, affects the heat uptake of the tropical oceans and the storage of extra heat due to greenhouse gas emissions, and hence plays a crucial role in the global climate system4–8. In addition, the ITF serves as the key to the Global Meridional Overturning Circulation (GMOC) system1,9,10. The strengthening and weakening of the ITF lead to a fluctuation of the inter-basin exchange between the Pacific and Indian Oceans, change the GMOC and shape the Indo-Pacific and global marine environment and climate6–8,11.

Previous studies suggest that the ITF possesses significant natural variability on multi-timescales, e.g., intra-seasonal variability triggered by the Madden-Julian Oscillation12, interannual variability associated with El Niño-Southern Oscillation13–17, decadal variability related to the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)11,18–23, as well as long-term changes due to external forcing4,24–26. Climate modes affect the ITF through both the wind forcing and salinity changes related to freshwater forcing11,16,27–29. The salinity effect plays an essential role in the interannual variability and decadal trend of the ITF transport and properties11,16. Recent studies suggest that the salinity effect is important in determining the multi-decadal change of the ITF as well30,31.

In the context of global warming, climate models suggest that the ITF will be weakened significantly due to a number of factors including a weakening of the Walker Circulation in the Pacific Ocean4; and/or a decrease in the deep waters entering the Pacific basin at ~40°S with subsequent reduction in the net deep ocean upwelling in the tropical and South Pacific24,32; and/or remote forcing in the North Atlantic Ocean26. It is worth noting that the ITF is in general affected by either wind forcing-related dynamics, and/or buoyancy-forcing related processes that primarily affect the halosteric component30. In contrast to the climate models, historical observations suggest that the ITF transport showed no significant trend during the past century or even an increasing trend during the recent decades when the ocean has been rapidly warming11,30,31,33,34. Given that greenhouse gas concentrations are expected to continue rising over the next century as they have over the past hundred years, the inconsistency between historical ITF trends and future projections raises critical questions. It is therefore essential to understand the response of ITF to rising greenhouse gas concentration, and at what threshold of greenhouse gas concentration will the long-term trend of ITF become discernible.

Several tipping points may be triggered when global temperatures rise above 1.5°C compared with the pre-industrial level35–37. Recent studies suggest that the increase of global temperature will exceed 1.5°C in less than 10 years according to the current emissions trajectory38. The ocean circulation system shows significant changes in response to global warming39, and the collapse of the AMOC is thought to be one of the most prominent climate tipping elements35–37,40,41. A long-term strengthening or weakening of the ITF could lead to state transitions of the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean (IPO) system: a strong ITF means extensive exchange of heat, fresh water, nutrients and carbon between the two oceans, while a collapsed ITF represents a relatively isolated IPO system. However, it remains uncertain whether the ITF can be classified as one of the tipping elements or not.

In this study, we aim to investigate the response of the ITF to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2), examine the independent responses of halosteric and thermosteric components of the ITF, and explore the role of the ITF as a potential climate tipping element, using numerical simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) and in situ observations.
paper_content.results:
We mainly use simulations from the historical runs (Hist, 1850–2014) and idealized 1% annually increasing CO2 concentrations experiments (1pctCO2, 1850–1999) from 25 CMIP6 coupled climate models to examine the ITF response to increasing CO2 concentration. First, we validated the ITF strength in the CMIP6 models and found that the multi-model mean reasonably reproduces the observed ITF30 and captures its mean structure and seasonal cycle. The vertical structure of the climatological mean zonal currents across the 114°E section and their changes in 1pctCO2 relative to the Hist runs are shown in Supplementary Fig. S1a. The mean ITF in the CMIP6 models shows a core between 11°S and 13°S with maximum velocity greater than 20 cm/s.

The ITF transport averaged over the 150 years in the Hist runs of CMIP6 is about −13 Sv (hereafter negative for westward into the Indian Ocean), quite close to the −15 Sv determined from direct observations42. Supplementary Fig. S1b presents a comparison of the seasonal cycle of ITF transports from the historical runs of CMIP6 models and the geostrophic calculations using observations-based datasets30. The observed seasonal cycle of ITF transports is well reproduced in the CMIP6 Hist runs. The correlation coefficient is 0.82 (significant at a 99% confidence level) between the ensemble mean of CMIP6 models and the observed geostrophic transport.

To separate the halosteric and thermosteric components, we calculated the total transport of the ITF and geostrophic transport of the ITF with modeled temperature and salinity. The time series of ITF transport in the 1pctCO2 experiments and Hist runs of CMIP6 and their halosteric (ITFS) and thermosteric (ITFT) components are presented in Fig. 1.

Although the geostrophic transport is smaller than the total transport, the ITF transports from the geostrophic calculations (Fig. 1a, d) are in good agreement with the total transport in both the 1pctCO2 experiments and the Hist runs (Supplementary Fig. S2), indicating that the geostrophic current is a major component of the ITF at 114°E.

The natural variation of the ITF transports, defined as the standard deviation of the detrended time series, is about 0.45 Sv in both the 1pctCO2 experiments and the Hist runs. However, the long-term trends in the 1pctCO2 experiments are clearly different from that in the Hist runs. As evident, the ITF transport in the Hist runs shows no significant trend during the past 150 years (Fig. 1d). By comparison, the ITF transport in the 1pctCO2 experiments shows a persistent weakening trend of about 0.3 Sv per decade, i.e., 4 Sv over 150 years, which is statistically significant at a 99% confidence level (Fig. 1a).

The trend of the ITF transport in the Hist runs is very weak and much smaller than the uncertainty: the linear trend of the total ITF is −0.01 ± 0.04 Sv decade−1 (positive for decreasing transport), the trend of ITF is −0.02 ± 0.13 Sv decade−1, while the linear trend of ITF is 0.01 ± 0.13 Sv decade−1 (Fig. 1f–h). By contrast, the ITF transport in the 1pctCO2 experiments shows a significant decreasing trend: the linear trend of total ITF is 0.28 ± 0.11 Sv decade−1, with the trend of ITF at −0.32 ± 0.37 Sv decade−1, while the linear trend of ITF is 0.60 ± 0.38 Sv decade−1. Hence, the halosteric and thermosteric components of the ITF transport show significant opposite trends in response to the increasing CO2 concentration.

Although the trends of ITF transport in Hist runs are much weaker than that in the 1pctCO2 experiments, the uncertainties in the two experiments have a similar order of O(0.1) Sv decade−1, and natural variability in the two experiments have the same magnitude (0.45 Sv) as well. This implies that the natural variability in the simulated ITF transport in the two experiments are comparable and reasonable, and the significant difference between the long-term trends in ITF transport is due to their difference in the external forcing, i.e., the CO2 concentrations in the two experiments.

The ITF transport and its halosteric and thermosteric components as a function of CO2 forcing are shown in Fig. 2. It should be noted that in CMIP6 models, the CO2 forcing is represented by the total atmospheric mass of CO2 (measured in Kg), which also serves as a variable indicating the concentration of atmospheric CO2. The thermosteric component of ITF transport shows a decreasing ITF transport trend with increased CO2 forcing at a rate of 0.86 Sv per 1015 Kg (Fig. 2c, b). By comparison, the halosteric ITF transport shows an increasing ITF transport trend with enhanced CO2 forcing at a rate of −0.37 Sv per 1015 Kg (Figs. 2c, b). As a result, the total ITF transport is decreased with CO2 forcing at a rate of approximately 0.62 Sv per 1015 Kg (Fig. 2a, b).

Interestingly, the decline of ITF transport in response to atmospheric CO2 forcing is weak when the CO2 mass is less than approximately 3 × 1015 Kg (i.e., 385 ppm, Supplementary Fig. S3a) or greater than 8 × 1015 Kg (red dots in Supplementary Fig. S3b), but is very rapid in between, indicating a nonlinear response of the ITF transport and its components to external CO2 forcing. The decline trend of total ITF (ITF) in response to CO2 forcing is 0.81 Sv per 1015 Kg when 3 × 1015 Kg < CO2 mass < 8 × 1015 Kg, but drops to 0.31 Sv per 1015 Kg when CO2 mass is greater than 8 × 1015 Kg, and 0.21 Sv per 1015 Kg when CO2 mass is less than 3 × 1015 Kg (Fig. 2b). The decline rate of the ITF shows a peak of 0.93 Sv per 1015 Kg when CO2 mass is about 4.5 × 1015 Kg, which is about 4 times of that when CO2 before 3 × 1015 Kg and 3 times of that when CO2 after 8 × 1015 Kg. These features suggest that a CO2 mass of ~3 × 1015 Kg and 8 × 1015 Kg might provide two important turning points (Fig. 2). The comparison between the ITF response to the CO2 forcing in the 1pctCO2 experiments and the Hist runs may explain why the ITF transport in the Hist runs shows no significant trend. As we can see in Fig. 2, the CO2 forcing in the Hist runs is mostly less than 3 × 1015 Kg below the first turning point, and hence the response of the ITF is certainly much weaker than that in the 1pctCO2 experiments.

In addition, the ITF transport versus global mean surface temperature (GMST), and GMST as a function of CO2 mass, is shown in Supplementary Fig. S4. We find that the GMST increases linearly with the increasing of CO2 mass with no turning points (Supplementary Fig. S4a), but the GMST shows a similar qualitative response as a function of CO2 concentration, with an initial slow response followed by a faster growth and two turning points (Supplementary Fig. S4b). The model spread in the simulated ITF-GMST relationship is notable, but the overall trend of ITF in response to GMST is much greater than the model spread (Supplementary Fig. S4b). The consistency of ITF-CO2 and ITF-GMST is not surprising, considering the linear relationship between GMST and CO2 mass. The ITF anomalies (minus their corresponding mean values) in three CO2 scenarios, including 1pctCO2, Hist, and the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 585, are plotted together for comparison, and these scenarios indicate a similar ITF response to CO2 forcing (Supplementary Fig. S4c).

To further examine the emerging time of the long-term trend of the ITF from its natural variability, we have calculated the running trend of the ITF transport over a 30-year window in both the CMIP historic runs and 1pctCO2 experiments. As shown in Supplementary Fig. S5, the running trend in the Hist runs fluctuates within a range of roughly −2 to 2 Sv/century, which is a result of natural variability. By contrast, in the 1pctCO2 experiments, the 30-year running trend reaches 4 Sv/century rapidly, and the fluctuations are masked by the significant decreasing trend when the CO2 reaches the first turning point, indicating that the first turning point is indeed the emerging time of a weakening ITF trend that is distinct from its natural variability.

Observations suggest that the CO2 mass has increased from 2.46 × 1015 Kg in 1958 to 3.10 × 1015 Kg in 2014, indicating an increasing rate of CO2 mass of about 1.12 × 1015 Kg per century during the past half a century (Supplementary Fig. S3). Observations indicate that the annual mean CO2 in 2023 was approximately 3.30 × 1015 Kg, which implies an increase of about 0.84 × 1015 Kg since 1958. With a mean rate of 0.42 Sv per 1015 Kg, the increase of CO2 by the year 2023 would lead to a decrease of about 0.4 Sv in the ITF transport, which is comparable to the natural variability, i.e., 0.45 Sv. Assuming a future rate of CO2 increase similar to that observed in 2014, the mass of CO2 would exceed 4.33 × 1015 Kg a century later. As shown in Fig. 2a, the ITF will finally be stable at only about 6.9 Sv when the CO2 is beyond 8.5 × 1015 Kg, indicating that the exchange between the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean would be nearly half of that at present, and the IPO system would be relatively isolated. This phase transition is hence essential for the Indo-Pacific environment and the global climate system.

A further question arises as to how the wind and buoyancy forcing, which exert direct control over variations in ITF transport, respond to external CO2 forcing. This is specifically relevant given that the ITF is determined by the Indo-Pacific pressure gradient related to the difference in steric height between the western Pacific Ocean and eastern Indian Ocean, which is further regulated by wind forcing and buoyancy forcing (precipitation) in the Indo-Pacific Ocean30.

Given that the ITF’s response is determined by the response of both the thermosteric component and halosteric component, we first examine the response of oceanic temperature and salinity in the Indo-Pacific Ocean to increasing CO2 concentration. Supplementary Fig. S6 presents the ensemble mean trends of temperature and salinity in the 1pctCO2 experiments, and the time series of temperature and salinity averaged over the western Pacific Ocean (WPO, 120–180°E, 15°S–15°N) and the eastern Indian Ocean (EIO, 80–114°E, 22°S–8°S) over the upper 200 m layer. Both the WPO and EIO show a significant warming trend in the 1pctCO2 experiments, but the warming in the EIO is much more rapid than that in the WPO, leading to a decreased temperature difference between the EIO and WPO with the increased CO2 concentration (Supplementary Fig. S6c and S6e). By contrast, the difference in salinity between the EIO and WPO is increased as the CO2 concentration increases due to a significant freshening in WPO but with no significant change in salinity in the EIO (Supplementary Fig. S6d and S6f).

Previous studies suggest that the temperature in the tropical Indo-Pacific Ocean is mainly related to a convergence of warm water due to zonal wind stress, while salinity changes in the upper layer ocean are mainly associated with surface freshwater input due to precipitation43,44. Hence, we further examine the response of the zonal wind stress and precipitation in the tropical Indo-Pacific Ocean to the CO2 forcing in the 1pctCO2 experiments.

As shown in Fig. 3, zonal wind stress in both the EIO and WPO show an increasing trend, i.e., weakening of westward trade winds, in the 1pctCO2 experiments, leading to a significant decreasing trend in the difference of zonal wind stress between the EIO and WPO. Note that, for the wind forcing, the ITF variability on decadal and longer timescales is likely controlled by mostly the Pacific winds and then the southeastern Indian Ocean6. The weakening of trade winds in the western Pacific Ocean leads to weakening convergence of warm water in the upstream region of the ITF in the Pacific and reduces the pressure gradient between the western Pacific Ocean and eastern Indian Ocean that drives the long-term ITF45. In comparison, the trends of precipitation in the two regions are clearly opposite: significantly increased precipitation in the WPO but decreased precipitation in the EIO. This opposite response causes an increasing trend of precipitation difference between the EIO and WPO (Fig. 3d). An intermediate point exists at 5 × 1015 kg of CO2, where the wind stress and precipitation anomaly changes sign, but this is mainly because we display anomalies relative to a mean value over a CO2 range of 2 to 10 × 1015 kg.

Like the ITF transport, the response of wind forcing and precipitation in the Indo-Pacific Ocean to CO2 forcing also shows turning points (Fig. 3b, d). During the stages with atmospheric CO2 mass less than 3 × 1015 Kg or massive atmospheric CO2 mass greater than 8 × 1015 Kg, the responses of both wind forcing and precipitation are weak. But between the two turning points, both the forcings, particularly the wind forcing, are very sensitive to the increasing of CO2 mass (Fig. 3b, d). After exceeding the second turning point, the responses of wind stress and precipitation differences in the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean to CO2 are both weakened, leading to a reduced ITF response, which may be associated with changes in the background state and the weakened Indo-Pacific exchange under this regime. Therefore, the responses of wind stress and precipitation to increasing CO2 concentration explain the opposite and nonlinear response of the ITF’s halosteric and thermosteric components to increasing CO2 concentration.
paper_content.methods:
Model outputs from the historical runs (Hist, 1850–2014) and idealized 1% annually increasing CO2 concentrations experiments (1pctCO2, 1850–1999) from 25 CMIP6 coupled climate models49 are used to investigate the response of ITF to external forcing. These models include: ACCESS-CM2, ACCESS-ESM1-5, CAMS-CSM1-0, CAS-ESM2-0, CESM2, CESM2-WACCM, CESM2-WACCM-FV2, CMCC-CM2-SR5, CMCC-ESM2, CanESM5, E3SM-1-0, EC-Earth3-AerChen, EC-Earth3-CC, EC-Earth3-Verg, FGOALS-f3-L, FIO-ESM-2-0, IPSL-CM5A2-INCA, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MCM-UA-1-0, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-HAM, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0, NESM3, and SAM0-UNICON. The 1pctCO2 is one of the four baseline experiments of the Diagnostic, Evaluation and Characterization of Klima (DECK) experiments, which is one of the three major components of CMIP. We used temperature, salinity, zonal and meridional current velocities, zonal and meridional components of wind stress, and precipitation from these models to investigate the responses of the halosteric and thermosteric components of the ITF to the increasing CO2 forcing.

Both the Hist and 1pctCO2 runs branch the end of the pre-industrial control (piControl runs) in 1850. The piControl reproduces an equilibrium state that lasts 500 years and serves as a baseline for branched experiments like the Hist and 1pctCO2. The forcing for Hist and 1pctCO2 runs are external forcing like emissions of greenhouse gases (GHGs) and aerosols due to human activities and volcanic eruptions. It should be noted that the external forcing for the Hist runs are based on observations over 1850–201450, and the Hist runs are usually used to examine natural variability and compare with historical observations17. For example, Santoso et al.17 found that the CMIP5 models overall simulate aspects of ITF variability. The 1pctCO2 runs branches the piControl as well, but are driven by idealized forcing that is the same as that in piControl except for the prescribed CO2 concentration increasing at 1% yr−1 (month by month or suddenly rises by 1% at the end of the year) since 1850 without considering any observations. So, the historical runs can be approximately regarded as an approximation of “real world”, while the 1pctCO2 runs are idealized experiments. Using the 1pctCO2 runs and their comparison with Hist runs, we are able to emulate the response of the ITF to an increasing of CO2 concentration.

In addition to the Hist runs and 1pctCO2 runs, simulations from the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 585 and forced by an abrupt quadrupling of CO2 (abrupt 4×CO2 runs) when available are employed as well. The geostrophic transport of ITF from Lu et al.30 (L24) is used for comparison to the numerical simulations. The geostrophic transport L24 was estimated using observation-based dataset products.

ITF transport
The ITF transport is calculated as the zonal transport across the 114°E section (8.5°S–22.5°S) bounded by Java and Australia, as defined in previous studies30:

\int_{8.5^{\circ}S}^{22.5^{\circ}S} \int_{0m}^{1100m} u dydz, (1)

where u is zonal current velocity, y and z denote meridional and vertical directions. Current velocities from the CMIP models and geostrophic current velocities calculated with oceanic temperature and salinity from the RG Argo Climatology and CMIP6 model outputs are used to compute the ITF transport. Here, we used the 1100 m as the level of no motion, considering the sill depth of ITF within the Indonesian Seas16. Using deeper depth as the level of no motion lead to no significant difference of the fluctuation of ITF transport.

Geostrophic current and its thermosteric and halosteric components
The zonal geostrophic velocity V between two adjacent stations of A and B is calculated by ref. 51

V = \frac{1}{fL} \int_{P_B}^{P_A} \alpha_A dp - \int_{P_B}^{P_A} \alpha_B dp, (2)

where f is the Coriolis parameter, L is the distance between A and B, P_A and \alpha_A are the pressure and the specific volume anomaly of A, respectively, P_B and \alpha_B are the same for B, P_r is the reference level of no flow and is designated as the 1100-m surface.

The thermosteric (S', T) and halosteric components (S, T') of the ITF are separated following Hu and Sprintall16, where T and S are time-dependent, and T' and S' are climatological means.

Data availability
CMIP6 model outputs, including the historical (Hist) runs, 1% annually increasing CO2 concentration experiments (1pctCO2), Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 585 and abrupt quadrupling of CO2 (abrupt 4×CO2) runs, are available at https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/. Monthly in-situ CO2 datasets are available at https://scrippsco2.ucsd.edu/. The geostrophic transport of Indonesian Throughflow from Lu et al. (2024) can be found at a repository site at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/Zenodo.17564268).

Code availability
Code and documentation for the CMIP6 models are publicly available at https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/. Model outputs were processed using the software MATLAB R2023a. The Matlab code for Figs. 2 and 3 is available at Github (https://github.com/ShijianHu/ITF). The code for the basemap (M_Map) is available at https://www-old.eoas.ubc.ca/~rich/map.html.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors used two CIMP6 simulations, the historical and 1% CO2 increase, to identify a nonlinear response of the ITF transport to the CO2 levels. They found a turning point in the rapid decline of the ITF at the current CO2 level and one at a high CO2 level when the decline in ITF becomes stable. The findings are new to the climate community and the topic is worthwhile for a quick publication.
Here are some comments for the authors to address before the manuscript can be finalized.
The authors propose that the current CO2 level is a turning point for the ITF. Is it also a turning point for other climate indices? could they be related to the ITF variation and change?
A few studies have examined the projected ITF changes under the RCP scenarios. For example, the CO2 levels in Fig. 2 may be related to what is expected by the end of this century.
Previous studies have related the ITF reduction to deep water mass and deep upwelling. It is useful to understand the connection between the surface circulation and the thermohaline circulation contribution.
Line 86-88: the CMIP models, with only greenhouse gas forcing, wouldn't be able to capture the interannual variations of the ITF in observation, which can only be captured with realistic wind forcing. By examining Fig. S1, the correlation is mostly due to the annual cycle of the ITF.
Fig. 3: there are studies suggesting the equatorial Indian Ocean winds are important for the ITF variability. So it's not clear the usefulness of using the 22-8S band to represent the Indian Ocean wind response.
In any case, the wind forcing may be secondary to the thermohaline forcing?
The lower panel of Fig. 4 shows the mean state, which doesn't illustrate the potential changes.
It would be nice to pinpoint the causes of a second turning point.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Using results from idealized CMIP6 annually 1% CO2 rise experiments, the authors have assessed the thermosteric and halosteric components of the ITF transport and concluded that the increasing CO2 concentration in the atmosphere shall eventually lead to a decline in ITF transport. The authors also proposed two turning points based on the changing rate of the ITF transport. The manuscript is generally well written except that the citation numbers are not correctly indexed and the figure captions need improvement. The findings are important but should be presented with the right context.
I have some significant concerns about the findings and the interpretations which are listed below. By addressing these concerns, the manuscript could be more rigorous, appropriately contextualized, and valuable to the scientific community.
Major Concerns:
1) The idealized 1% CO2 rise experiment used in the study neglects other anthropogenic sources of radiative forcing, such as aerosols. Since aerosols, which are on a declining trend, counteract some of the warming effects of increasing CO2, this could bias the results, and the proposed vanishing ITF transport might be expedited under more realistic conditions. The authors could address this concern by acknowledging that the 1% CO2 experiment is a simplification and that, in reality, aerosols and other factors (such as land use changes and different greenhouse gases) might influence the rate and magnitude of ITF transport changes. The authors should clarify that their results represent an idealized scenario and not a direct prediction of future conditions, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive modeling that incorporates multiple forcings. They should also discuss the potential uncertainties in their conclusions, given the absence of realistic time-evolving aerosol and other greenhouse gas forcing in the experiment.
2) The study assumes a fixed level of no motion at 1100 m, but the bathymetry at 114 E reaches much deeper (~6000 m) between 11S – 22S. Recent studies have shown significant barotropic variabilities in the Indo-Pacific basin (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsr.2023.104104), suggesting that the level of no motion should extend to the ocean bottom for more accurate transport estimates. This may become all the more relevant with the impending climate change wherein frequent extreme events are predicted. An atmospheric disturbance can generate barotropic responses if the wavenumber and the frequency meet certain criteria (see M.J. Lighthill, Time-varying currents, Philos. Trans. Roy. Soc. Lond. Math. Phys. Sci., 270 (1971), pp. 371-390). The authors should consider adjusting their ITF transport calculation to account for deeper bathymetry, potentially extending the level of no motion to the ocean bottom. They could discuss how this adjustment would likely improve the accuracy of the total ITF transport estimates. I do understand that any additional experiment with CMIP6 is time and resource consuming. The authors should at the least present a sensitivity analysis based on the revised assumption of the level of no motion and show that extending the bathymetry to the ocean bottom does not significantly alter the findings of this study.
3) The causality of the declining ITF transport lies in the changing wind stress and precipitation. Figure 3b and 3d represent a turning point (5 x 1015 kg CO2) where the wind stress and precipitation anomaly changes sign. Why the turning point related to wind stress and precipitation anomalies (as shown in Figures 3b and 3d) is not considered more relevant than the two turning points proposed by the authors. The concern is that the authors may have missed a potentially important relationship between the changes in wind stress and precipitation and the ITF transport. The authors could revise their interpretation of the turning points and consider whether the changes in wind stress and precipitation are more directly tied to the decline in ITF transport than the two turning points they originally proposed.
4) I have concerns that the abstract may sensationalize the findings, suggesting an imminent and rapid decline in ITF transport. The authors should carefully revise the abstract to better reflect the idealized nature of the study and clarify that the findings pertain to a specific experimental scenario rather than an immediate real-world prediction.
Minor Comments:
1) Line 39-42 : The authors may wish to apprise the readers about the MJO driven ITF transports.
2) Line 52-53: If the winds are strong enough, it can affect the entire water depth.
3) Line 62: It will be good to inform the readers about the time needed for the global temperature to reach 1.5 C given the current trend.
4) Captions in Fig S1(a) and Fig S1(b) appear to be swapped. Caption mentions cm/s whereas the colorbar appears in m/s.
5) The authors use the abbreviations in tandem without describing it. For example, MITF is used in the Results section but it is described much later in the Methods.
6) Line 77: Even though CMIP6 is pretty well known across the earth science community, it is a good practice to expand the initials given the varied reader base of this journal.
7) Line 88-90: What is the correlation between the ITF transport from CMIP6 and MITF and the level of significance ? The authors should mention it in the caption of Figure S1b if not in the text.
8) Line 95-97 : The magnitude differs by ~ 3 Sv. The trends appear similar though. The authors should mention it apart from highlighting that the two transports are in good agreement.
9) Line 108-112: Why does not ITF_T and ITF_S add up to the total ITF given that the residual term is negligible as claimed in Hu and Sprintall 2016.
10) ITF’ used in Fig S2b and S2d is not defined anywhere.
11) Fig 2: The shades in Fig 2b should be properly described in the caption.
12) Fig 2(a) : 1pctCO2 -EN ??? What does it refer to ?
13) Line 184-187: I suppose that the temperature and salinity is averaged over depth. If yes, it is averaged up to what depth ? These details should be mentioned in the text.
14) Figure S4 : I don’t see black quadrilaterals in panels (a) and (c).
15) Fig 3: Captions (b) and (c) should state that the points are from all CMIP6 models. In fact, the authors should be more attentive about the captions across all figures.
16) Line 241 : Typo.... Change existed to exist.
17) Figure 4 should be described in some detail in the text rather than leaving it to the interpretation of the readers.
18) Line 266-268 : “We find that the response of zonal wind stress in the Indo-Pacific Ocean is featured by nonlinear weakening trend with two turning points like ITF’s response”. This statement is based on Figure 3. It’s not clear from the plot why those two points should be called turning points.
19) Line 329 : The indexed reference is actually number 15 instead of 14.
20) Line 287-289 : It is important to elaborate how CO2 increment is implemented in the models. Are the 1% increments spread over months or sudden at the end of a year ? What about the other greenhouse gases? Not all readers may be aware of the DECK experiments within the CMIP6 framework. The manuscript will be more complete if these relevant details are mentioned instead of directing the readers to ref no 47.
21) Since this journal admits 10 display figures, I don’t see a need to include Supplementary Figures in this manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Review of “Imminent rapid decline of the Indonesian Throughflow after reaching a turning point of CO2 concentration”, by Shijian Hu et al.
Submitted to Nature Communications
This manuscript discusses the response of the Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) to increasing CO2, in 25 CMIP6 climate models. The model runs studied are the historical (HIST) and 1% per annum CO2 increase (1pctCO2) runs. The manuscript notes that when plotted against CO2 concentration the ITF response is nonlinear, with an initially slow rate of weakening, which accelerates and then slows again as a function of CO2 concentration. The second part of the paper begins to unpick some of the mechanisms of the ITF decline, finding that a balance/competition between wind-driven differences in warming, and precipitation-driven changes in salinity, appear to be the main drivers of the ITF weakening. The authors conclude by speculating, based on the 1pctCO2 results, that current CO2 concentrations may be such that a rapid weakening of the ITF may be imminent.
.
The topic of the paper, changes in the ITF in response to increasing greenhouse gas forcing, is interesting and important, and to the best of my knowledge has not been extensively studied in the literature to date. So the study is welcome.
Unfortunately there are some methodological weaknesses in the analysis which to my mind invalidate the discussion of the nonlinear response and the conclusion that a rapid ITF decline may be imminent. I have noted these under ‘Methodological issues’ below. I did find the discussion of mechanisms of ITF weakening interesting and more convincing.
Overall, my feeling is that the authors have the basis of a valuable and interesting study, particularly on the mechanisms driving the ITF weakening, but that a large part of the analysis presented, and the conclusions drawn from it, need to be revisited, to the extent that any revised version would essentially be a different paper. Hence I cannot recommend acceptance of this paper, but I hope that the authors will continue with this work and in particular publish and develop further their analysis of mechanisms. Noting the dependence on supplementary figures, it may be that this analysis would work best in a longer format journal.
I’m sorry I can’t be more positive about the present manuscript, but I hope that these comments are useful and constructive in taking this interesting work forward.
Methodological issues
Apart from Fig. 1, the authors present their analysis of the 1pctCO2 run in terms of CO2 concentration rather than time (Figs 2-4). They note a levelling off of the ITF weakening at higher concentrations. This is entirely to be expected as the radiative forcing from CO2 increases logarithmically with the concentration. Indeed this is why the standard protocol follows a percentage increase of concentration per year rather than a linear increase. The same levelling off would be seen in any climate variable (e.g. global mean temperature), if plotted against CO2 concentration. Since there is no direct mechanistic link between CO2 concentration and ITF (only the indirect link through the response of the climate system), it really makes no sense to plot the response in this way.
The above does not explain the initial slow response of the ITF. This can equally well be seen when plotting the response against time (Fig. 1a). This is most likely an issue of the initial response time to perturbations. Other variables such as global mean temperature show a 2-timescale response to CO2 perturbations, with a fast timescale of a decade or two followed by a longer adjustment time. It is seen most clearly in the instantaneous 4xCO2 experiment but is also there in the 1pctCO2 experiments (see e.g. https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/clim/26/6/jcli-d-12-00195.1.xml ). This initial adjustment time may be different for the ITF than for global mean temperature, and in fact understanding this response time would be a valuable addition to the mechanistic analysis in this study. In any case, it seems a priori far more likely that the initial slow response is related to an inherent timescale of the model dynamics rather than a specific threshold CO2 concentration. The apparent ‘threshold’ CO2 concentration would therefore be entirely dependent on the specific timeseries of concentration used to force the model. I think if the claim that there is a specific threshold CO2 concentration that results in acceleration is to be made, it would at least have to be shown across several different CO2 forcing scenarios.
Following on from the above, the claim in the Discussion section that the real ITF may be on the verge of a rapid decline, based on current CO2 concentrations, is not justified. Even if CO2 concentration were somehow the direct control variable (which hasn’t been demonstrated), what about all the other radiatively active forcing species in the present and future atmosphere? In any case, to assess the claim, why not simply look at the projection runs (ScenarioMIP) to see if the models actually project a rapid ITF decline?

change?

rapidly weakened and the Indo-Pacific Ocean is going to be in a state with weak inter-

turning point for other climate indices related to ITF.

changes in CO2 concentration would lead to changes in the inter-basin exchange of
heat and freshwater between the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean, turning points might

A few studies have examined the projected ITF changes under the RCP scenarios. For
example, the CO2 levels in Fig. 2 may be related to what is expected by the end of this
century. Previous studies have related the ITF reduction to deep water mass and deep

Response: Yes, some previous studies have examined the projected ITF changes by the
end of this century under the RCP scenarios. As you note, several previous studies have
examined the relationship between the ITF reduction and deep ocean circulation (i.e.,
related to deep water mass and deep upwelling) as well (Sen Gupta et al. 2016; Feng et
al. 2017). For example, Feng et al. (2017) examined the annual mean ITF volume
transport in the historical and RCP8.5 runs using a near-global 1/10° ocean general
circulation model, and suggested that deep ocean circulation, through changes in net
deep ocean upwelling in the tropical and South Pacific, is as important as wind-driven
processes to the ITF transport and variability. Sen Gupta et al. (2012) suggested that
the ITF reduction in the CMIP3 models might result from a weaker Mindanao Current
transport given that the changes in the two transports have similar magnitudes. As
pointed by Sprintall et al (2024), “One alternative hypothesis suggested for the ITF
transport weakening is a projected reduction in the upwelling and circulation of the
deep waters entering the Pacific from the Southern Ocean that ultimately upwell to exit
via the ITF (Sen Gupta et al. 2016; Feng et al. 2017).” So, changes in the deep ocean
circulation might indeed play an important role in the low-frequency variability and
long-term trend of ITF. In any case, whether ITF changes are generated by the wind or
by the deep-upwelling related to thermohaline circulation, would be contained in the
changes of Indo-Pacific pressure gradient.
In the revised manuscript, we have added a few sentences to discuss the connection
between the surface circulation and the thermohaline circulation contribution and the
potential role of deep-water mass and deep upwelling in the ITF reduction.

model forcing and sensitivity are consistent with the observational record, which
provides opportunities to better bound the magnitude of aerosol forcing (e.g. Stevens,

2015).” Hence, the CMIP historical simulations are usually used to examine natural
variability and compare with historical observations. For example, Santoso et al. (2022)

Response: Thanks for your question. Yes, some studies suggest that the equatorial
Indian Ocean winds are important for the ITF variability, but this is dependent on the
specific time scales. Please note that the ITF flows into the Indian Ocean in the southern
hemisphere within the latitudes of 22-8°S, and the major mechanism that the equatorial
Indian Ocean winds influence the ITF is through generating equatorial Kelvin waves
which propagate to the equatorial eastern Indian Ocean and then southward to the ITF
region along the coasts. This means that the influence of the equatorial Indian Ocean
winds on the ITF variability is relatively confined in the time scales of Kelvin waves
(typically range from intra-seasonal, seasonal to interannual time scales).
On longer time scales, things are quite different. For example, Sprintall et al. (2009)
found that “To first order, the seasonal cycle of transport in the thermocline (_100–150
m) in all three exit straits is dominated by regional monsoon forcing, with maximum
ITF during the southeast monsoon.” On decadal time scales, the ITF variability is likely
controlled by mostly the Pacific winds and then the southeastern Indian Ocean.
For example, Lee et al. (2015) carried out sensitivity experiments to understand the relative
importance of wind forcing from the different ocean basins in driving the ITF variability,
and they conclude that “Using real-time surface winds inside the Pacific Ocean and
climatological winds outside of the Pacific Ocean (EXP_PAC), the abrupt increase of
the Indian OHC700during the 2000s was successfully simulated.”

relative contribution of the wind forcing and the thermohaline forcing to the ITF change.

have assessed the thermosteric and halosteric components of the ITF transport and
concluded that the increasing CO2 concentration in the atmosphere shall eventually
lead to a decline in ITF transport. The authors also proposed two turning points based
on the changing rate of the ITF transport. The manuscript is generally well written
except that the citation numbers are not correctly indexed and the figure captions need
improvement. The findings are important but should be presented with the right context.

listed below. By addressing these concerns, the manuscript could be more rigorous,
appropriately contextualized, and valuable to the scientific community.
Response: Thank you for your encouragement and constructive suggestions. We have
made careful revisions according to your comments, and the citation numbers have been
corrected, the figure captions have been improved. Please see our point-by-point
responses below.
Major Concerns:
1) The idealized 1% CO2 rise experiment used in the study neglects other
anthropogenic sources of radiative forcing, such as aerosols. Since aerosols, which are
on a declining trend, counteract some of the warming effects of increasing CO2, this
could bias the results, and the proposed vanishing ITF transport might be expedited
under more realistic conditions. The authors could address this concern by
acknowledging that the 1% CO2 experiment is a simplification and that, in reality,
aerosols and other factors (such as land use changes and different greenhouse gases)
might influence the rate and magnitude of ITF transport changes. The authors should
clarify that their results represent an idealized scenario and not a direct prediction of
future conditions, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive modeling that
incorporates multiple forcings. They should also discuss the potential uncertainties in
their conclusions, given the absence of realistic time-evolving aerosol and other
greenhouse gas forcing in the experiment.

forcing, such as aerosols; and neglecting these anthropogenic sources may counteract

your suggestions, we have:

primarily affect the Earth's climate system through the radiative balance and energy
budget, as the reviewer points out. The ITF, as one component of the climate system,
therefore responds to CO₂ indirectly—through adjustments such as the modified
regional differences in warming and also through salinity changes. Therefore, when we

consistently demonstrates a nonlinear response to CO₂, the existence of two turning
points, and a significant weakening trend between them. While climate models
inevitably have their limitations, the ones used here represent the current state-of-the-
art in simulating the Earth's climate system. We strive to understand future climate
changes and pursue perfectly accurate results, but this is the most advanced level we
can achieve at present.

tipping points—while observational data simultaneously indicate that CO₂

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Review of “Imminent rapid decline of the Indonesian Throughflow after reaching a turning point of CO2 concentration”, by Shijian Hu et al.
Submitted to Nature Communications
This is my third review of this manuscript. I thank the authors for their careful responses to my last set of comments, including performing substantial additional analyses. I think these analyses, shown in new supplementary figures, shed further light on what is going on. Unfortunately I still find the framing of the results in the main text of the manuscript unconvincing, so I can’t recommend publication it its current form. I do think there is a way forward to produce a highly impactful paper, but it would be more of a rewrite than a revision.
First I have some comments on the new supplementary figures:
Fig. S4(a) (plot of ITF against GMST), This apparently shows an initial slow response of the ITF to increasing GMST. If real, to me this is more unexpected and more striking than the low-CO2 response in the plot of ITF against CO2 concentration (Fig. 2a), which as discussed in my earlier reviews might be expected due to the initial slow warming in the 1% runs. Presumably a slow ITF response at lower warming levels is due to lags in the system such as the multi-decadal adjustment time of the ITF to instantaneous radiative forcing (new Fig. S7). However as it stands I don’t find Fig. S4 convincing. It shows no data for GMST <3.5 deg C. I would expect it to go right down to GMST=0, as there is plenty of data at these GMST values available in the 1pctCO2 runs. The figure also needs an indication of the ensemble spread or confidence interval for the ensemble mean values shown. Because there is a large range in the Transient Climate Response (TCR) between the models (see IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7), a given GMST value is likely to be reached at very different CO2 concentrations between models, so a fairly large spread is to be expected. These additions are needed to convince the sceptical reader that the apparent slow initial response is real.
Fig. S7 (Response of ITF in the instantaneous 4xCO2 runs). The response is very interesting here, showing that the (ensemble mean) ITF stabilises at ~6Sv after a few decades, even though the GMST is still warming at this point in most/all of the runs. This does provide evidence (more convincing evidence than Fig. 2a) that a levelling off of the ITF at a non-zero value can be expected at some future point. I think this behavior potentially sheds valuable light on the response dynamics of the ITF. A more in-depth process analysis to determine what sets the timescale and the stabilisation level would be very valuable, building on the insights to the wind and buoyancy forcings in the manuscript. To facilitate this it would be important to show how much the stabilisation time and level vary among the ensemble members/models.
Fig. S8 (ITF as a function of CO2 in HIST and SSP585 runs). By eye I can’t see a clear discontinuity in the slope between the HIST and SSP585 segments. Given the large ensemble spread (evident from the individual plots in the figure), and noise even in the ensemble mean, I doubt that there is any statistically or practically significant difference. The final drop in the timeseries (and in the rate of change in panel b) looks like an edge effect (noting that similar drops are seen at earlier points in the figure, e.g. around CO2 = 650 and 850 ppm). To me, this figure does not as it stands support the assertion in the title of “imminent rapid decline of the ITF”.
The new figures have started to unpack some potentially very interesting behavior, and have the potential to really move forward understanding of the future of the ITF. The evidence presented suggests that the response of the ITF to increasing CO2 is dependent on the history of CO2 forcing as well as the current concentration, due to the significant delay timescales of both surface temperature and the ITF itself. This means that conclusions drawn purely from analysis of the 1% CO2 runs are strongly contingent on that specific forcing scenario. It might be more convincing if the SSP585 and 1% timeseries could be plotted together, using consistent processing methods (e.g. it looks as if Figs 2a and S8 use different smoothing), and with a realistic estimate of uncertainty/ensemble spread.
In short, I think the figures (including the new supplementary figures) contain a lot of valuable information about the response of the ITF to a warming climate, although some need a little more work to be convincing. The initial response seems to be a combination of more than one dynamical delay timescales, and so is particularly dependent on forcing scenario, while the later levelling off of the ITF response looks like a more robust feature. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The Indonesian Throughflow (ITF) represents the only tropical inter-ocean pathway of global ocean circulation and plays a central role in the Earth’s climate system. Climate models suggest that the ITF would be weakened under global warming, but historical observations indicate a contradictory trend. Here using CMIP6 simulations, we find that the response of the ITF to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration is nonlinear and exhibits an abrupt rapid decline after surpassing a turning point. The ITF’s decline can be explained by the response of its halosteric and thermosteric components to rising CO2 levels associated with changes in winds and precipitation. The current level of CO2 concentration has reached the turning point, indicating that a rapid decline of ITF and a transition of the Indo-Pacific state is likely imminent despite the remaining uncertainties. These findings have implications for understanding climate tipping elements and global ocean circulation under global warming.

---

## Introduction

The Indo-Pacific region is the only pathway that connects different ocean basins in the tropics and plays a central role in the Earth’s climate system1–3. The cross-basin oceanic flow from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean, termed the Indonesian Throughflow (ITF), controls the inter-ocean exchange of heat and fresh water between the Pacific Ocean and Indian Ocean, affects the heat uptake of the tropical oceans and the storage of extra heat due to greenhouse gas emissions, and hence plays a crucial role in the global climate system4–8. In addition, the ITF serves as the key to the Global Meridional Overturning Circulation (GMOC) system1,9,10. The strengthening and weakening of the ITF lead to a fluctuation of the inter-basin exchange between the Pacific and Indian Oceans, change the GMOC and shape the Indo-Pacific and global marine environment and climate6–8,11.

Previous studies suggest that the ITF possesses significant natural variability on multi-timescales, e.g., intra-seasonal variability triggered by the Madden-Julian Oscillation12, interannual variability associated with El Niño-Southern Oscillation13–17, decadal variability related to the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) and the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)11,18–23, as well as long-term changes due to external forcing4,24–26. Climate modes affect the ITF through both the wind forcing and salinity changes related to freshwater forcing11,16,27–29. The salinity effect plays an essential role in the interannual variability and decadal trend of the ITF transport and properties11,16. Recent studies suggest that the salinity effect is important in determining the multi-decadal change of the ITF as well30,31.

In the context of global warming, climate models suggest that the ITF will be weakened significantly due to a number of factors including a weakening of the Walker Circulation in the Pacific Ocean4; and/or a decrease in the deep waters entering the Pacific basin at ~40°S with subsequent reduction in the net deep ocean upwelling in the tropical and South Pacific24,32; and/or remote forcing in the North Atlantic Ocean26. It is worth noting that the ITF is in general affected by either wind forcing-related dynamics, and/or buoyancy-forcing related processes that primarily affect the halosteric component30. In contrast to the climate models, historical observations suggest that the ITF transport showed no significant trend during the past century or even an increasing trend during the recent decades when the ocean has been rapidly warming11,30,31,33,34. Given that greenhouse gas concentrations are expected to continue rising over the next century as they have over the past hundred years, the inconsistency between historical ITF trends and future projections raises critical questions. It is therefore essential to understand the response of ITF to rising greenhouse gas concentration, and at what threshold of greenhouse gas concentration will the long-term trend of ITF become discernible.

Several tipping points may be triggered when global temperatures rise above 1.5°C compared with the pre-industrial level35–37. Recent studies suggest that the increase of global temperature will exceed 1.5°C in less than 10 years according to the current emissions trajectory38. The ocean circulation system shows significant changes in response to global warming39, and the collapse of the AMOC is thought to be one of the most prominent climate tipping elements35–37,40,41. A long-term strengthening or weakening of the ITF could lead to state transitions of the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean (IPO) system: a strong ITF means extensive exchange of heat, fresh water, nutrients and carbon between the two oceans, while a collapsed ITF represents a relatively isolated IPO system. However, it remains uncertain whether the ITF can be classified as one of the tipping elements or not.

In this study, we aim to investigate the response of the ITF to increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2), examine the independent responses of halosteric and thermosteric components of the ITF, and explore the role of the ITF as a potential climate tipping element, using numerical simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) and in situ observations.

---

## Results

We mainly use simulations from the historical runs (Hist, 1850–2014) and idealized 1% annually increasing CO2 concentrations experiments (1pctCO2, 1850–1999) from 25 CMIP6 coupled climate models to examine the ITF response to increasing CO2 concentration. First, we validated the ITF strength in the CMIP6 models and found that the multi-model mean reasonably reproduces the observed ITF30 and captures its mean structure and seasonal cycle. The vertical structure of the climatological mean zonal currents across the 114°E section and their changes in 1pctCO2 relative to the Hist runs are shown in Supplementary Fig. S1a. The mean ITF in the CMIP6 models shows a core between 11°S and 13°S with maximum velocity greater than 20 cm/s.

The ITF transport averaged over the 150 years in the Hist runs of CMIP6 is about −13 Sv (hereafter negative for westward into the Indian Ocean), quite close to the −15 Sv determined from direct observations42. Supplementary Fig. S1b presents a comparison of the seasonal cycle of ITF transports from the historical runs of CMIP6 models and the geostrophic calculations using observations-based datasets30. The observed seasonal cycle of ITF transports is well reproduced in the CMIP6 Hist runs. The correlation coefficient is 0.82 (significant at a 99% confidence level) between the ensemble mean of CMIP6 models and the observed geostrophic transport.

To separate the halosteric and thermosteric components, we calculated the total transport of the ITF and geostrophic transport of the ITF with modeled temperature and salinity. The time series of ITF transport in the 1pctCO2 experiments and Hist runs of CMIP6 and their halosteric (ITFS) and thermosteric (ITFT) components are presented in Fig. 1.

Although the geostrophic transport is smaller than the total transport, the ITF transports from the geostrophic calculations (Fig. 1a, d) are in good agreement with the total transport in both the 1pctCO2 experiments and the Hist runs (Supplementary Fig. S2), indicating that the geostrophic current is a major component of the ITF at 114°E.

The natural variation of the ITF transports, defined as the standard deviation of the detrended time series, is about 0.45 Sv in both the 1pctCO2 experiments and the Hist runs. However, the long-term trends in the 1pctCO2 experiments are clearly different from that in the Hist runs. As evident, the ITF transport in the Hist runs shows no significant trend during the past 150 years (Fig. 1d). By comparison, the ITF transport in the 1pctCO2 experiments shows a persistent weakening trend of about 0.3 Sv per decade, i.e., 4 Sv over 150 years, which is statistically significant at a 99% confidence level (Fig. 1a).

The trend of the ITF transport in the Hist runs is very weak and much smaller than the uncertainty: the linear trend of the total ITF is −0.01 ± 0.04 Sv decade−1 (positive for decreasing transport), the trend of ITF is −0.02 ± 0.13 Sv decade−1, while the linear trend of ITF is 0.01 ± 0.13 Sv decade−1 (Fig. 1f–h). By contrast, the ITF transport in the 1pctCO2 experiments shows a significant decreasing trend: the linear trend of total ITF is 0.28 ± 0.11 Sv decade−1, with the trend of ITF at −0.32 ± 0.37 Sv decade−1, while the linear trend of ITF is 0.60 ± 0.38 Sv decade−1. Hence, the halosteric and thermosteric components of the ITF transport show significant opposite trends in response to the increasing CO2 concentration.

Although the trends of ITF transport in Hist runs are much weaker than that in the 1pctCO2 experiments, the uncertainties in the two experiments have a similar order of O(0.1) Sv decade−1, and natural variability in the two experiments have the same magnitude (0.45 Sv) as well. This implies that the natural variability in the simulated ITF transport in the two experiments are comparable and reasonable, and the significant difference between the long-term trends in ITF transport is due to their difference in the external forcing, i.e., the CO2 concentrations in the two experiments.

The ITF transport and its halosteric and thermosteric components as a function of CO2 forcing are shown in Fig. 2. It should be noted that in CMIP6 models, the CO2 forcing is represented by the total atmospheric mass of CO2 (measured in Kg), which also serves as a variable indicating the concentration of atmospheric CO2. The thermosteric component of ITF transport shows a decreasing ITF transport trend with increased CO2 forcing at a rate of 0.86 Sv per 1015 Kg (Fig. 2c, b). By comparison, the halosteric ITF transport shows an increasing ITF transport trend with enhanced CO2 forcing at a rate of −0.37 Sv per 1015 Kg (Figs. 2c, b). As a result, the total ITF transport is decreased with CO2 forcing at a rate of approximately 0.62 Sv per 1015 Kg (Fig. 2a, b).

Interestingly, the decline of ITF transport in response to atmospheric CO2 forcing is weak when the CO2 mass is less than approximately 3 × 1015 Kg (i.e., 385 ppm, Supplementary Fig. S3a) or greater than 8 × 1015 Kg (red dots in Supplementary Fig. S3b), but is very rapid in between, indicating a nonlinear response of the ITF transport and its components to external CO2 forcing. The decline trend of total ITF (ITF) in response to CO2 forcing is 0.81 Sv per 1015 Kg when 3 × 1015 Kg < CO2 mass < 8 × 1015 Kg, but drops to 0.31 Sv per 1015 Kg when CO2 mass is greater than 8 × 1015 Kg, and 0.21 Sv per 1015 Kg when CO2 mass is less than 3 × 1015 Kg (Fig. 2b). The decline rate of the ITF shows a peak of 0.93 Sv per 1015 Kg when CO2 mass is about 4.5 × 1015 Kg, which is about 4 times of that when CO2 before 3 × 1015 Kg and 3 times of that when CO2 after 8 × 1015 Kg. These features suggest that a CO2 mass of ~3 × 1015 Kg and 8 × 1015 Kg might provide two important turning points (Fig. 2). The comparison between the ITF response to the CO2 forcing in the 1pctCO2 experiments and the Hist runs may explain why the ITF transport in the Hist runs shows no significant trend. As we can see in Fig. 2, the CO2 forcing in the Hist runs is mostly less than 3 × 1015 Kg below the first turning point, and hence the response of the ITF is certainly much weaker than that in the 1pctCO2 experiments.

In addition, the ITF transport versus global mean surface temperature (GMST), and GMST as a function of CO2 mass, is shown in Supplementary Fig. S4. We find that the GMST increases linearly with the increasing of CO2 mass with no turning points (Supplementary Fig. S4a), but the GMST shows a similar qualitative response as a function of CO2 concentration, with an initial slow response followed by a faster growth and two turning points (Supplementary Fig. S4b). The model spread in the simulated ITF-GMST relationship is notable, but the overall trend of ITF in response to GMST is much greater than the model spread (Supplementary Fig. S4b). The consistency of ITF-CO2 and ITF-GMST is not surprising, considering the linear relationship between GMST and CO2 mass. The ITF anomalies (minus their corresponding mean values) in three CO2 scenarios, including 1pctCO2, Hist, and the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 585, are plotted together for comparison, and these scenarios indicate a similar ITF response to CO2 forcing (Supplementary Fig. S4c).

To further examine the emerging time of the long-term trend of the ITF from its natural variability, we have calculated the running trend of the ITF transport over a 30-year window in both the CMIP historic runs and 1pctCO2 experiments. As shown in Supplementary Fig. S5, the running trend in the Hist runs fluctuates within a range of roughly −2 to 2 Sv/century, which is a result of natural variability. By contrast, in the 1pctCO2 experiments, the 30-year running trend reaches 4 Sv/century rapidly, and the fluctuations are masked by the significant decreasing trend when the CO2 reaches the first turning point, indicating that the first turning point is indeed the emerging time of a weakening ITF trend that is distinct from its natural variability.

Observations suggest that the CO2 mass has increased from 2.46 × 1015 Kg in 1958 to 3.10 × 1015 Kg in 2014, indicating an increasing rate of CO2 mass of about 1.12 × 1015 Kg per century during the past half a century (Supplementary Fig. S3). Observations indicate that the annual mean CO2 in 2023 was approximately 3.30 × 1015 Kg, which implies an increase of about 0.84 × 1015 Kg since 1958. With a mean rate of 0.42 Sv per 1015 Kg, the increase of CO2 by the year 2023 would lead to a decrease of about 0.4 Sv in the ITF transport, which is comparable to the natural variability, i.e., 0.45 Sv. Assuming a future rate of CO2 increase similar to that observed in 2014, the mass of CO2 would exceed 4.33 × 1015 Kg a century later. As shown in Fig. 2a, the ITF will finally be stable at only about 6.9 Sv when the CO2 is beyond 8.5 × 1015 Kg, indicating that the exchange between the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean would be nearly half of that at present, and the IPO system would be relatively isolated. This phase transition is hence essential for the Indo-Pacific environment and the global climate system.

A further question arises as to how the wind and buoyancy forcing, which exert direct control over variations in ITF transport, respond to external CO2 forcing. This is specifically relevant given that the ITF is determined by the Indo-Pacific pressure gradient related to the difference in steric height between the western Pacific Ocean and eastern Indian Ocean, which is further regulated by wind forcing and buoyancy forcing (precipitation) in the Indo-Pacific Ocean30.

Given that the ITF’s response is determined by the response of both the thermosteric component and halosteric component, we first examine the response of oceanic temperature and salinity in the Indo-Pacific Ocean to increasing CO2 concentration. Supplementary Fig. S6 presents the ensemble mean trends of temperature and salinity in the 1pctCO2 experiments, and the time series of temperature and salinity averaged over the western Pacific Ocean (WPO, 120–180°E, 15°S–15°N) and the eastern Indian Ocean (EIO, 80–114°E, 22°S–8°S) over the upper 200 m layer. Both the WPO and EIO show a significant warming trend in the 1pctCO2 experiments, but the warming in the EIO is much more rapid than that in the WPO, leading to a decreased temperature difference between the EIO and WPO with the increased CO2 concentration (Supplementary Fig. S6c and S6e). By contrast, the difference in salinity between the EIO and WPO is increased as the CO2 concentration increases due to a significant freshening in WPO but with no significant change in salinity in the EIO (Supplementary Fig. S6d and S6f).

Previous studies suggest that the temperature in the tropical Indo-Pacific Ocean is mainly related to a convergence of warm water due to zonal wind stress, while salinity changes in the upper layer ocean are mainly associated with surface freshwater input due to precipitation43,44. Hence, we further examine the response of the zonal wind stress and precipitation in the tropical Indo-Pacific Ocean to the CO2 forcing in the 1pctCO2 experiments.

As shown in Fig. 3, zonal wind stress in both the EIO and WPO show an increasing trend, i.e., weakening of westward trade winds, in the 1pctCO2 experiments, leading to a significant decreasing trend in the difference of zonal wind stress between the EIO and WPO. Note that, for the wind forcing, the ITF variability on decadal and longer timescales is likely controlled by mostly the Pacific winds and then the southeastern Indian Ocean6. The weakening of trade winds in the western Pacific Ocean leads to weakening convergence of warm water in the upstream region of the ITF in the Pacific and reduces the pressure gradient between the western Pacific Ocean and eastern Indian Ocean that drives the long-term ITF45. In comparison, the trends of precipitation in the two regions are clearly opposite: significantly increased precipitation in the WPO but decreased precipitation in the EIO. This opposite response causes an increasing trend of precipitation difference between the EIO and WPO (Fig. 3d). An intermediate point exists at 5 × 1015 kg of CO2, where the wind stress and precipitation anomaly changes sign, but this is mainly because we display anomalies relative to a mean value over a CO2 range of 2 to 10 × 1015 kg.

Like the ITF transport, the response of wind forcing and precipitation in the Indo-Pacific Ocean to CO2 forcing also shows turning points (Fig. 3b, d). During the stages with atmospheric CO2 mass less than 3 × 1015 Kg or massive atmospheric CO2 mass greater than 8 × 1015 Kg, the responses of both wind forcing and precipitation are weak. But between the two turning points, both the forcings, particularly the wind forcing, are very sensitive to the increasing of CO2 mass (Fig. 3b, d). After exceeding the second turning point, the responses of wind stress and precipitation differences in the western Pacific and eastern Indian Ocean to CO2 are both weakened, leading to a reduced ITF response, which may be associated with changes in the background state and the weakened Indo-Pacific exchange under this regime. Therefore, the responses of wind stress and precipitation to increasing CO2 concentration explain the opposite and nonlinear response of the ITF’s halosteric and thermosteric components to increasing CO2 concentration.

---

## Methods

Model outputs from the historical runs (Hist, 1850–2014) and idealized 1% annually increasing CO2 concentrations experiments (1pctCO2, 1850–1999) from 25 CMIP6 coupled climate models49 are used to investigate the response of ITF to external forcing. These models include: ACCESS-CM2, ACCESS-ESM1-5, CAMS-CSM1-0, CAS-ESM2-0, CESM2, CESM2-WACCM, CESM2-WACCM-FV2, CMCC-CM2-SR5, CMCC-ESM2, CanESM5, E3SM-1-0, EC-Earth3-AerChen, EC-Earth3-CC, EC-Earth3-Verg, FGOALS-f3-L, FIO-ESM-2-0, IPSL-CM5A2-INCA, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MCM-UA-1-0, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-HAM, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0, NESM3, and SAM0-UNICON. The 1pctCO2 is one of the four baseline experiments of the Diagnostic, Evaluation and Characterization of Klima (DECK) experiments, which is one of the three major components of CMIP. We used temperature, salinity, zonal and meridional current velocities, zonal and meridional components of wind stress, and precipitation from these models to investigate the responses of the halosteric and thermosteric components of the ITF to the increasing CO2 forcing.

Both the Hist and 1pctCO2 runs branch the end of the pre-industrial control (piControl runs) in 1850. The piControl reproduces an equilibrium state that lasts 500 years and serves as a baseline for branched experiments like the Hist and 1pctCO2. The forcing for Hist and 1pctCO2 runs are external forcing like emissions of greenhouse gases (GHGs) and aerosols due to human activities and volcanic eruptions. It should be noted that the external forcing for the Hist runs are based on observations over 1850–201450, and the Hist runs are usually used to examine natural variability and compare with historical observations17. For example, Santoso et al.17 found that the CMIP5 models overall simulate aspects of ITF variability. The 1pctCO2 runs branches the piControl as well, but are driven by idealized forcing that is the same as that in piControl except for the prescribed CO2 concentration increasing at 1% yr−1 (month by month or suddenly rises by 1% at the end of the year) since 1850 without considering any observations. So, the historical runs can be approximately regarded as an approximation of “real world”, while the 1pctCO2 runs are idealized experiments. Using the 1pctCO2 runs and their comparison with Hist runs, we are able to emulate the response of the ITF to an increasing of CO2 concentration.

In addition to the Hist runs and 1pctCO2 runs, simulations from the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 585 and forced by an abrupt quadrupling of CO2 (abrupt 4×CO2 runs) when available are employed as well. The geostrophic transport of ITF from Lu et al.30 (L24) is used for comparison to the numerical simulations. The geostrophic transport L24 was estimated using observation-based dataset products.

ITF transport
The ITF transport is calculated as the zonal transport across the 114°E section (8.5°S–22.5°S) bounded by Java and Australia, as defined in previous studies30:

\int_{8.5^{\circ}S}^{22.5^{\circ}S} \int_{0m}^{1100m} u dydz, (1)

where u is zonal current velocity, y and z denote meridional and vertical directions. Current velocities from the CMIP models and geostrophic current velocities calculated with oceanic temperature and salinity from the RG Argo Climatology and CMIP6 model outputs are used to compute the ITF transport. Here, we used the 1100 m as the level of no motion, considering the sill depth of ITF within the Indonesian Seas16. Using deeper depth as the level of no motion lead to no significant difference of the fluctuation of ITF transport.

Geostrophic current and its thermosteric and halosteric components
The zonal geostrophic velocity V between two adjacent stations of A and B is calculated by ref. 51

V = \frac{1}{fL} \int_{P_B}^{P_A} \alpha_A dp - \int_{P_B}^{P_A} \alpha_B dp, (2)

where f is the Coriolis parameter, L is the distance between A and B, P_A and \alpha_A are the pressure and the specific volume anomaly of A, respectively, P_B and \alpha_B are the same for B, P_r is the reference level of no flow and is designated as the 1100-m surface.

The thermosteric (S', T) and halosteric components (S, T') of the ITF are separated following Hu and Sprintall16, where T and S are time-dependent, and T' and S' are climatological means.

Data availability
CMIP6 model outputs, including the historical (Hist) runs, 1% annually increasing CO2 concentration experiments (1pctCO2), Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) 585 and abrupt quadrupling of CO2 (abrupt 4×CO2) runs, are available at https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/. Monthly in-situ CO2 datasets are available at https://scrippsco2.ucsd.edu/. The geostrophic transport of Indonesian Throughflow from Lu et al. (2024) can be found at a repository site at Zenodo (doi:10.5281/Zenodo.17564268).

Code availability
Code and documentation for the CMIP6 models are publicly available at https://aims2.llnl.gov/search/cmip6/. Model outputs were processed using the software MATLAB R2023a. The Matlab code for Figs. 2 and 3 is available at Github (https://github.com/ShijianHu/ITF). The code for the basemap (M_Map) is available at https://www-old.eoas.ubc.ca/~rich/map.html.
